Slide 1 - Title
Medical Oncology Terminology by Halima Ba MPH, MD, Affordable Language Services (08/29/2013).
Slide 2 - Oncology / Oncologist
Oncology: The study of tumors, both malignant and benign. Oncologist: A doctor who specializes in
treating cancer.
Slide 3 - Cancer Definition
Cancer is an abnormal cell division without control and cells are able to invade other tissues. Cancer
cells can spread to other parts of the body through the blood and lymph systems.
Slide 4 - Blood and Lymphatic Systems
Cancer uses the cardiovascular and lymphatic systems as primary pathways for regional and distant
metastasis throughout the body.
Slide 5 - Types of Tumors
Benign tumors are not cancerous. Malignant tumors are cancerous. Some cancers do not form solid
tumors; for example, leukemia is a cancer of the bone marrow and blood.
Slide 6 - Cancer Statistics
In 2013, an estimated 11,630 cases of cancer diagnosed in children 14 and younger compared to over
1.6 million cases diagnosed in adults (National Cancer Institute).
Slide 8 - Most Common Childhood Cancers in USA
Leukemia: 31% of all childhood cancers (including benign brain tumors); Brain and other CNS tumors:
25%; Neuroblastoma: 6%; Wilms tumor: 5%; Non-Hodgkin lymphoma: 4%; Hodgkin lymphoma: 4%;
Rhabdomyosarcoma: 3%; Osteosarcoma: 3%; Retinoblastoma: 2%; Ewing sarcoma: 1%.
Slide 9 - Etiology of Childhood Cancers
Causes are largely unknown. Down syndrome, other chromosomal/genetic abnormalities, and ionizing
radiation exposures explain a small percentage of cases.
Slide 10 - Most Common Adult Cancers in USA

According to the National Institutes of Health: Lung and bronchial cancer, Colon and rectal cancer,
Breast cancer, Pancreatic cancer, Prostate cancer, Leukemia, Non-Hodgkin lymphoma, Liver and
intrahepatic bile duct cancer, Ovarian cancer, Esophageal cancer.
Slide 11 - Etiology of Adult Cancer
Major causal categories: Environmental factors, Viruses and bacteria, Lifestyle factors, Medical drugs
and hormones, Hereditary/genetic factors.
Slide 12 - Environmental Factors
Industrial/occupational exposures: Coal miners, factory workers, asbestos. Ultraviolet light increases
risk of skin cancers. Ionizing radiation (X-rays, nuclear accidents) increases risk of breast cancer,
leukemia, and thyroid cancer.
Slide 13 - Viruses and Bacteria in Cancer
Epstein-Barr virus (EBV): Hodgkin lymphoma. Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV): NHL and Kaposi
sarcoma. Human Papillomavirus (HPV): Cervical cancer. Hepatitis B and C: Hepatocellular cancer.
Human T-cell leukemia virus (HTLV-1): Risk of leukemia and lymphoma. Helicobacter pylori (HP):
Stomach cancer.
Slide 15-16 - Lifestyle Factors
Tobacco / Cigarette smoking causes lung, oropharyngeal, and bladder cancers. Radon causes lung
cancer. Alcohol is associated with esophageal, liver, oropharynx, breast, and larynx cancers. Diet high
in fat and low in fruits and vegetables is implicated in colorectal cancer.
Slide 17 - Drugs and Hormones Causing Cancer
Alkylating agents (Cyclophosphamide, Melphalan): Bladder cancer, leukemia. Antimetabolites
(Azathioprine): NHL, skin cancer. Corticosteroids (Prednisone): NHL. Estrogens (Diethylstilbestrol):
Vaginal cancer in female offspring. Combined chemotherapy and radiation: Secondary leukemia.
Slide 18 - Hereditary / Genetic Syndromes
Cancer as primary manifestation: Retinoblastoma, neuroblastoma, pheochromocytoma. Inherited
conditions: Familial polyposis, Fanconi anemia, Xeroderma pigmentosum. Immune deficiencies:
Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome. Chromosomal aberrations: Down syndrome.
Slide 19 - Cancer Warning Signs & Symptoms
A thickening or lump in the breast or any other part of the body; A new mole or change in existing mole
(ABCDE); A sore that does not heal; Hoarseness or cough that does not go away; Changes in bowel or
bladder habits; Discomfort after eating or difficulty swallowing; Unexplained weight loss or gain;
Unusual bleeding or discharge; Feeling weak or very tired.
Slide 20-21 - Screening Protocols

Breast: Mammogram is the best tool to find breast cancer early (X-ray picture of the breast). Cervix:
Pap test (Pap smear) checks cervical cells; start 3 years after sexual intercourse or at age 21, repeated
every 3 years. Colon and rectum: Screening tests detect polyps and cancer for adults aged 50 and
older.
Slide 22-27 - Diagnostic Modalities
Biopsy: Removal of small section of tumor for histopathological analysis (needle biopsy, resection
biopsy). Hematology: Measures blood cells, bone marrow aspiration, lumbar puncture for spinal fluid.
Tumor markers: Neuron-specific enolase (NSE) for neuroblastoma; Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) for germ
cell/liver tumors. Medical Imaging: X-ray, CT (cross-sectional computer slices), MRI (magnetic
resonance of biochemical tissue activity), Ultrasound (sound wave reflection).
Slide 28-29 - Cancer Staging Systems
TNM Staging: T (Size/extent of primary tumor), N (Number and regional lymph nodes involved), M
(Distant metastasis). Summary Stage: Stage 0 (in situ), Stage I (local stage), Stage II (local or regional
depending on nodes), Stage III (regional stage), Stage IV (distant metastasis).
Slide 32-37 - Cancer Treatments
Surgery: Pre-operative chemotherapy shrinks tumor before surgery; Complete resection removes entire
tumor; Prosthesis/Endoprosthesis replaces amputated bone/limb. Radiotherapy: External radiotherapy
from outside source; Internal radiotherapy / Brachytherapy places radioactive source inside or near
tumor; Systemic radiation travels via liquid/capsule; Total Body Irradiation (TBI) destroys malignant
cells before Bone Marrow Transplant (BMT). Chemotherapy: Cytotoxic drugs kill or damage rapidly
dividing cells; Central line (e.g., Hickman catheter) delivers chemo directly into central vein. Hormone
therapy: Drugs block hormone production/action; Surgery removes hormone-producing ovaries/testes.
Bone Marrow Transplant: Allogeneic BMT uses matched donor marrow; Autologous BMT uses patient's
own treated marrow; Peripheral Blood Stem Cell Rescue (PBSC).
Slide 38 - Toxicity and Side Effects
Acute side effects: Transient, sudden or severe. Chronic side effects: Long-lasting (e.g., kidney
damage, heart toxicity). Immunosuppression: Dampened immune system making patient prone to
infections. Neutropenia: Low white blood cell count (febrile neutropenia when accompanied by fever).
Slide 39 - Prognosis Terminology
Remission: Symptoms and evidence of cancer disappear under clinical testing. Relapse: Disease
reoccurs after remission period. Refractory: Cancer is resistant to treatment and does not respond.
Restaging: Staging evaluation repeated after therapy to measure response. Follow-up: Periodic visits to
monitor and detect recurrence early.
Slide 40 - Breast Cancer Five-Year Survival Rates
Stage 0 (DCIS): 93%; Stage I: 88%; Stage IIA: 81%; Stage IIB: 74%; Stage IIIA: 67%; Stage IIIB: 41%;
Stage IIIC: 49%; Stage IV (Metastatic): 15%.

Slide 44-48 - Medical Oncology Vocabulary
Carcinogenesis: development of cancer. Apoptosis: programmed normal restraining cell death.
Neoplasm: tumor. Carcinoma: cancer from skin or tissue lining organs (subtypes: adenocarcinoma,
basal cell, squamous cell, transitional cell). Sarcoma: cancer from bone, cartilage, muscle, blood
vessels (chondrosarcoma, hemangiosarcoma, mesothelioma). Lymphoma: cancer of
immune/lymphatic system. Leukemia: cancer of blood-forming bone marrow tissue. Myeloma: cancer of
plasma cells in bone marrow. Grading: degree of dedifferentiation (anaplasia) I to IV (IV most
abnormal). CIS: carcinoma in situ. Lumpectomy: tumor removal. Radical mastectomy: removal of
breast. Margins: borders of normal tissue around tumor. 3DCRT: 3D conformal radiation. IMRT:
intensity-modulated radiation therapy. Brachytherapy: internal radiation implants. Gamma knife
surgery: focused radiation for brain tumors. CAM: complementary and alternative medicine. Anaplasia:
loss of structural differentiation. Dysplastic: abnormal cell formation, not clearly malignant. Fungating:
mushrooming tumor growth. Laparoscopy: visual exam of abdominal cavity. Oncogenes:
cancer-causing mutated genes.
Slide 49-51 - Medical Suffixes in Oncology
-able (to be), -al (pertaining to), -ectomy (surgical excision), -emia (blood condition), -gen (produces),
-gene (gene), -gram (record/picture), -graphy (process of recording), -ic/-ical (pertaining to), -itis
(inflammation), -logy (study of), -oid (resembling), -oma (tumor/mass), -opsy (viewing), -osis
(condition/process), -pathy (disease), -plasia (condition of growth), -plasm (formed substance/growth),
-scopy (visual examination), -stasis (standing still/stopping), -therapy (treatment), -tomy
(incision/cutting).
